children: India’s electrical equipment industry is entering a phase where opportunity may no longer be its biggest constraint. As domestic power investment accelerates and companies pursue larger markets, the harder task is building organisations capable of absorbing rapid growth without weakening balance sheets, culture or execution.

For Siddharth Bhutoria, President-elect, IEEMA and Whole-time Director, RTS Power Ltd., financial discipline sits at the heart of that transition. “Cash flow, I think, in our industry has been a big, big pain point,” he said, pointing out that several companies that have successfully reached billion-dollar scale have maintained healthy balance sheets and relatively low leverage.

The environment itself has changed sharply. Bhutoria said the electrical equipment sector struggled to attract financing and investor interest until relatively recently, but the past five years have altered that perception. The opportunity now is substantial, but companies need to change the way they approach growth rather than simply expand existing operations.

One of the first hurdles is escaping commoditisation. “It’s very difficult to get a differentiated product,” Bhutoria said, describing a market where multiple manufacturers compete and domestic procurement can often be driven by L1 tendering. RTS Power’s own internationalisation required the company to move away from treating exports as an outlet for spare domestic capacity.

That shift also required operational separation. Bhutoria said attempting to manufacture for Indian and international standards within the same factory created problems, eventually prompting the company to dedicate a plant exclusively to exports. The experience illustrates a larger challenge for growing Indian companies: scale increasingly requires organisational redesign rather than simply additional capacity.
Growth Without Overstretching The Balance Sheet

Hartek India’s journey presents the same challenge from the perspective of an enterprise that grew from a small electrical equipment trading business into a roughly Rs 1,000 crore company. Hartek Singh, Director, Hartek India Pvt. Ltd., said the company progressively moved into turnkey solutions, substations, state utilities and subsequently renewable-energy infrastructure.

The company entered renewables around 2010, initially working with projects of only a few megawatts before scaling alongside the sector. Singh said Hartek has moved from building small substations to becoming an approved vendor for 765 kV substations and now aspires to become a billion-dollar company by 2030.

Yet Singh argued that pursuing every available contract would have jeopardised that journey. “We never tried to go overboard despite whatever opportunities were lying there,” he said. The constraint was not necessarily finding demand, but ensuring that available financial resources could sustain the pace of expansion.

“The biggest challenge for our kind of industry is cash flow,” Singh said. Skilled manpower represents the other major constraint, particularly for companies outside India’s largest industrial talent hubs. For an MSME attempting to become a much larger enterprise, therefore, the ability to finance and staff growth can matter as much as the size of the addressable market.

APAR Industries offers another version of the scaling problem: how an established company continues reinventing itself instead of plateauing. Rishabh Desai, Director, APAR Industries Ltd., described a business whose capabilities have accumulated across generations, beginning with conductors before expanding into transformer oils and cables.

That history has increasingly allowed APAR to combine businesses rather than operate them independently. In data centres, for instance, the company can participate through conductors carrying electricity to the facility, transformer oils and CTC, cables used inside the facility and newly developed server-cooling fluids.

“We’re no longer just selling one product, we’re selling you an energy infrastructure solution,” Desai said. The strategy allows a company approaching seven decades of existence to use capabilities accumulated over time to address a customer through multiple parts of the electricity infrastructure chain.
When Scale Becomes An Institutional Challenge

Desai also pointed to culture as an important part of sustaining rapid expansion. “People and culture make an organisation,” he said, noting that APAR has employees who have remained with the company for three or four decades. During periods of hypergrowth, such employees become carriers of institutional knowledge and culture as organisations recruit rapidly.

For Rohit Pathak, CEO, Birla Copper, Hindalco Industries Ltd., this institutional question becomes even more important as companies reach much larger scale. Rapid hiring can increase headcount, but unless culture remains consistent across plants and business verticals, expansion itself can become difficult to manage.

Governance is equally central to the transition. “Governance is something which can enable and unlock growth for you at a level, at a scale, that you never thought of,” Pathak said. Governance, he argued, affects not merely compliance but a company’s ability to raise capital, serve customers and operate within increasingly complex supply chains.

“If you don’t have that governance, you will not get to that scale,” Pathak said. Hindalco’s experience, he added, has been an attempt to combine professional management with what he described as “entrepreneurialism at scale”.

The scale of investment now underway illustrates why those systems matter. Pathak said Birla Copper is investing around Rs 15,000–20,000 crore across recycling, downstream products and upstream capacity to serve the Indian market, while giving individual businesses and management teams room to operate entrepreneurially.

The next generation of Indian electrical equipment giants may therefore be shaped by something less visible than factories or order books. With demand and investment opportunities expanding, the dividing line could increasingly be whether companies can build the cash-flow discipline, culture, governance and management systems required to grow without allowing that growth to overwhelm the organisation.
